issues: whether a refugee tribunal applied a standard of proof higher than the 'realistic possibility' of persecution required under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

whether the tribunal properly assessed the reasonableness of an internal relocation alternative, including the claimant's safety, cost of living, discrimination against non-indigenous persons, and ability to integrate in the proposed city
whether a refugee claimant's sworn testimony must be corroborated by independent evidence or can stand on its own as the basis for a finding of a well-founded fear of persecution
whether the tribunal erred in discounting expert psychological evidence on the basis that it rested on a single short assessment by a non-treating clinician
the standard of review applicable to a refugee tribunal's findings of fact and law, and the scope of a court's power to set aside those findings
whether the tribunal properly considered country condition evidence, including the reach of political connections and the capacity of a national police network to locate a person in any city

whether the combination of a forced female genital mutilation demand, a witchcraft accusation based on a traditional oracle, and police involvement constitutes a well-founded fear of persecution on a protected ground
key_facts: claimant fled a large West African city with two young daughters
husband's extended family demanded FGM for the girls and accused her of witchcraft on the word of a traditional oracle
family reported her to police; husband questioned for approximately two hours about her whereabouts
no further police contact in roughly ten months
claimant fears a specific uncle with political campaign connections could locate her in any city
claimant fears the national police computer network would enable officers to find her anywhere
tribunal found internal relocation to another major city was reasonable
tribunal discounted evidence of the uncle's reach as thin and inconsistent
tribunal noted husband's affidavit did not mention the uncle or the interrogation
tribunal found discrimination against non-indigenous persons and high cost of living did not make relocation unreasonable given her education and the family's successful business
tribunal gave little weight to a psychologist's report diagnosing depression and PTSD, noting it rested on a single one-hour assessment by a non-treating clinician
causes_of_action: judicial review of a refugee tribunal decision (reasonableness standard)
candidate_statutes: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27
Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7
